caption:
Apple cut the daily AI spending cap for some engineers from $300 to $200 last month, Bloomberg reported.
It is weighing $100 for some engineering teams and as little as $25 for some other groups.
The cuts are part of a wider cost push under CEO John Ternus.

threads_text: Apple cut some engineers' daily AI budget from $300 to $200, and may go to $100, Bloomberg reported. Some non-engineering teams could get just $25 a day. The tokenmaxxing era might be ending. Should your boss cap how much AI you can use?

site_article.headline: Apple cuts employee AI budgets as part of a cost-control push
site_article.dek: Some engineers saw their daily AI spending cap drop from $300 to $200, and some other teams could fall to $25, Bloomberg reported.
site_article.summary: Apple has lowered the daily AI usage budget for some engineers from $300 to $200 and is considering further cuts, Bloomberg News reported on November 4, 2026. The move is part of wider cost cutting under chief executive John Ternus.
site_article.seo_title: Apple cuts employee AI budgets, some engineers to $200 a day
site_article.seo_description: Apple lowered some engineers' daily AI cap from $300 to $200 and may cut further, to $25 for some teams, Bloomberg reported.
site_article.answer_summary: According to Bloomberg, Apple cut the daily AI spending allowance for some engineers from $300 to $200 in October and is considering $100 for some engineering teams and as little as $25 for some non-engineering groups.
site_article.hero_alt: An engineer at a cluttered desk with a laptop and a nearly empty coin jar, a large logo on the wall.

paragraphs.text: Apple has reduced the amount of money some employees can spend each day on AI tools, Bloomberg News reported on November 4, 2026, citing people familiar with the matter. Reuters and several technology outlets followed the report. Apple did not immediately respond to a Reuters request for comment, and an Apple spokesperson declined to comment to Bloomberg, according to PYMNTS.

In October, Apple cut the daily AI spending allowance for some engineers from $300 to $200, according to the report. The company is now considering lowering the limit for some engineering teams to $100 a day.

Many groups outside engineering already work under a $100 daily cap, and Apple has considered reducing that to as little as $25 for some teams. Employees who need more access can seek exemptions from senior executives, Reuters reported.

The budgets are measured in tokens, the units of data that AI models process and that providers bill for. Reuters named OpenAI's ChatGPT, Anthropic's Claude and Google's Gemini as examples of such models, and 9to5Mac reported that Apple employees have access to all three, although it was unclear exactly which tools the new limits cover. Some teams are being encouraged to switch to cheaper models or to models that run locally on their own devices.
Part of a wider cost push

9to5Mac reported that the change is part of broader cost cutting led by John Ternus, who now runs Apple as chief executive. Apple's research and development spending rose 32% to about $45.8 billion in fiscal 2026, partly because of higher infrastructure and AI costs, according to 9to5Mac and TipRanks.

Bloomberg reported that few workers were using their full $300 daily allowance, so it is unclear how much Apple will save, according to 9to5Mac. PYMNTS said employee reactions were mixed, with some staff worried that the limits point to broader cost cutting and possible layoffs. TipRanks noted that Apple has not announced layoffs tied to the AI limits.

Apple is not alone. PYMNTS listed other companies with AI usage limits, including a $200 weekly limit at Tesla and a $1,500 monthly limit at Uber. Reuters noted that Bloomberg recently reported Goldman Sachs had restricted access to some AI coding tools after reviewing productivity and risk management.

In NeuraFeed's reading, the report marks a shift in how large companies treat AI tools at work. After a period in which heavy token use was encouraged as a sign of productivity, the bills are now large enough that finance teams are setting limits and steering staff toward cheaper or on-device models.
The next sign to watch is whether the $100 and $25 caps take effect, and whether other large employers follow with similar limits in their own budgets.
